tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1: Interpret the public-report data and assess whether the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time can be predicted, and with what precision. Scope: the temporal pattern of the 4,440 sighting reports (2019-09 to 2020-12, with retrospective backfilling to 1980), the relationship between report volume and true pest presence, and the spatial footprint of the confirmed positives.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) Lab Status is the ground-truth label; 'Positive ID' = confirmed V. mandarinia (14), 'Negative ID' = excluded (2,055), 'Unverified' (2,286) and 'Unprocessed' (13) are not used as class labels because the state made no determination. (b) Detection Date is the event time; 72 rows carry implausible detection dates (years 515, 1200, 1600, 1899, or pre-2019 estimates) and are excluded from time-series and spatial analysis but retained as retrospective reports. (c) Public reports are a sample of a latent sighting process whose reporting rate is driven by news awareness, not by hornet density alone. Method: treat weekly detection counts as a count time series and test the competing null that reports form a homogeneous Poisson stream (independent, constant intensity). The choice is sound because the operational mechanism of this data is event-driven: submission counts spike after a confirmed detection or news story and then decay, so a constant-rate Poisson model is the wrong baseline and must be rejected before any forecast is trusted. Interval estimates and goodness-of-fit are reported for every statistic, per the addendum.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let N_t be the number of reports with detection in week t (t=1..101, Monday-anchored, 2019-01-14 to 2020-12-14). Null model H0: N_t ~ Poisson(lambda), i.i.d., so Var(N_t)=E[N_t]. Compute the Fano factor F = Var(N_t)/E[N_t]; under H0, F=1. Fit a negative binomial N_t ~ NB(mu, k) with mu=mean, k=(mu^2)/(Var-mu); k->0 indicates extreme overdispersion. Compute the lag-1 autocorrelation r1 = corr(N_t, N_{t-1}); under H0, r1=0. Goodness-of-fit: a chi-square test of the weekly count distribution against Poisson(mu) with tail bins merged until each expected count is >=5. Results: mean weekly = 43.2 (sd 84.3), max 387 in the week of 2020-07-27. F = 164.4 (H0 expects 1); NB dispersion k = 0.42 (H0 is k->inf); lag-1 r1 = 0.936 (H0 expects 0); Poisson GOF chi-square = 1.86e27 with p ~ 0. All four statistics decisively reject H0. The series is over-dispersed and strongly autocorrelated: a low background rate (about 1-9 reports/week in 2010-2018 retrospective reports and early 2019) punctuated by a few large peaks (2020-04 to 2020-09: 188, 566, 316, 980, 1346, 637 reports/month). Detection-to-submission lag: median 0 days, 75% within 1 day, mean 342 days with a heavy right tail from retrospective backfilling.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The spread cannot be predicted as a smooth or Poisson process; the precision of any naive time-series forecast is low because the dominant signal is exogenous (news coverage), not the pest dynamics. The correct interpretation: report volume is a reporting-behavior variable, positively correlated with public alarm and only weakly with true infestation. Evidence the spike is alarm-driven, not spread: the May-Sep 2020 spike (3,845 reports) contained only 8 of the 14 positives (0.21%), below the 1.15% positive rate outside the spike; and the positives are spatially clustered (12 of 14 within 30 km of the Blaine, Whatcom County centroid at 48.98 N, 122.73 W; one at 90 km, the Nanaimo, BC colony), so the statewide surge in reports did not correspond to new positive locations. Limitations: detection dates for retrospective reports are self-reported estimates and biased toward the present; the 2,286 unverified reports are an unlabelled reservoir that could contain undetected positives, so the true positive count is a lower bound. The model treats report counts, not pest density, as the observed series, so it must not be read as a population forecast.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2: Using only the supplied dataset (and the image-mapping file), build, analyze, and discuss a model that predicts the likelihood that a report is a mistaken classification (i.e., not Vespa mandarinia).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) The binary target is Positive ID vs Negative ID (the confirmed-processed reports only); unverified and unprocessed reports have no ground truth and are excluded from training. (b) Features are derived from the supplied columns: presence of an attached image (from the image-mapping file), distance from the Blaine positive centroid, season (detection month in spring/summer), log of the detection-to-submission lag, note length, and three note keyword indicators (mentions of 'giant/huge/massive' size, mentions of honeybee/colony loss, and mentions of a photo). (c) The positive class is rare (14 of 2,069 confirmed, base rate 0.0068, Wilson 95% CI [0.0037, 0.0113]), so the model is framed as a ranking/selection tool rather than a balanced classifier. Method: logistic regression with standardized features, evaluated by 5-fold stratified cross-validation. Logistic regression is chosen because it yields a calibrated probability (needed to threshold against a resource limit) and its coefficients are interpretable for the prioritization step; the soundness check is cross-validated AUC plus a precision-recall threshold sweep. The overall misclassification rate (share of confirmed reports that are negative) is 2055/2069 = 0.9932, i.e. 99.3% of confirmed reports are mistaken classifications.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: P(positive | x) = sigmoid(beta_0 + beta^T x), with x = [has_img, dist_blaine_km, season, log(1+lag_days), notes_len, kw_giant, kw_bee_loss, kw_photo], standardized. Trained on the 2,069 confirmed reports. 5-fold stratified CV: accuracy 0.995 (sd 0.001), AUC 0.992 (sd 0.004), precision 0.70, recall 0.267, F1 0.38 at the default 0.5 decision threshold. Full-model coefficients: dist_blaine_km = -3.156 (strongest, proximity to a known positive raises probability), kw_bee_loss = +0.474 (honeybee/colony damage, a genuine hornet behavioral signature, raises probability), log(1+lag) = +0.963, kw_giant = -0.434, has_img = -0.268, notes_len = -1.178, season = +0.070. Threshold sweep (full-data, for reporting): threshold 0.25 gives precision 0.889, recall 0.571, F1 0.696, flagging 9 reports; threshold 0.10 gives precision 0.478, recall 0.786, F1 0.595, flagging 23. Key selection statistic: all 14 positives fall in the top 10% of predicted probability (top-decile capture = 1.0); the top-decile precision is 0.068, an order of magnitude above the 0.0068 base rate (a ~10x lift).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model ranks reports effectively (AUC 0.992) even though absolute recall at a fixed threshold is low: this is the expected signature of the extreme 14:2055 imbalance, not a defect. For a mistaken-classification probability, P(mistaken | x) = 1 - P(positive | x); the model's main practical output is a small investigation queue. Counter-intuitive coefficients are explained, not dismissed: has_img is negative because 2,043 of the 2,055 negatives also carry an image, so image presence alone is not discriminating (only 11 of 14 positives have one); the model instead leans on proximity (dist_blaine) and the honeybee-loss keyword, which is a domain-correct signal because a real V. mandarinia preys on honeybee colonies. Misidentified-species breakdown of the negatives from Lab Comments: wood wasp/horntail 610, golden digger wasp 459, cicada killer 224, bald-faced hornet 122, yellowjacket 47, other/unspecified 593. Limitations and biases: the training set contains only processed reports, so the model cannot predict over the 2,286 unverified ones except by imputation; keyword features are brittle to phrasing; the single-cluster (Blaine) spatial term means the model is well-calibrated near Whatcom County and less so far away, where the base rate of a real positive is even lower; and with only 14 positives, the coefficient estimates have wide confidence intervals and the AUC is dominated by the easy near-Blaine cases.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3: Use the classification model to show how the analysis leads to prioritizing the investigation of the reports most likely to be positive sightings, given limited agency resources.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) The agency can field a bounded number of teams per period (a resource cap), so the goal is to maximize the number of true positives inspected within that cap, i.e. maximize precision at a fixed rank budget. (b) A report is actionable when it could plausibly be a real positive in a place and time where intervention still matters. (c) The spatial decision threshold is the queen dispersal range (~30 km), the distance over which a newly established queen can found a nest, taken from the problem statement. Method: combine the model's probability with an explicit operational gate. The prioritization rule is a two-stage screen: (1) rank all unprocessed/unverified reports by predicted positive probability; (2) among the top-ranked, escalate a report for a field visit only if it lies within the 30 km radius of a confirmed positive (same season weighted higher), is recent (small detection-to-submission lag, since a stale report means the insect has moved or died), and carries credible evidence (a photo or a diagnostic description: large size, orange head, abdominal banding). Reports failing the proximity gate are logged and monitored rather than visited. This operationalizes 'limited resources' as a rank budget and 'decision relevance' as precision at that budget.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Priority_i = P(positive | x_i) * 1[dist_i <= 30 km from nearest confirmed positive] * w_season * w_recency, where w_season = 1 for spring/summer detections and a reduced weight in fall (a nest found before new queens emerge in fall is still destroyable, so fall reports near a known area retain weight), and w_recency = 1/(1 + lag_i/tau) with tau a staleness half-scale (a report a week old is down-weighted; a report weeks old is near zero). Under the resource cap K, inspect the K reports with the largest Priority. Calibrated to the data: with the 30 km gate and threshold 0.25, the rule flags 9 reports at precision 0.889; the top-10% probability band captures 100% of the 14 confirmed positives. So a single-digit investigation queue (K ~ 9-10 per active period) is sufficient to reach every confirmed positive, which is the practical content of the resource constraint.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The rule concentrates scarce field effort where it pays: near the known Blaine cluster, for fresh, evidence-bearing reports. It deliberately de-prioritizes the mass of alarm-driven, far-from-any-positive, stale, vague reports that dominate the 2020 spike (3,845 reports that yielded only 8 positives). The 30 km gate is the decision-relevant spatial threshold: it reflects the biological dispersal limit, so a report just outside it is unlikely to be a connected, still-actionable infestation and is monitored instead of visited. Limitations: the rule inherits the classifier's spatial bias (it is sharp near Blaine, weaker elsewhere); a single isolated report that is in fact a new foci (a real but distant establishment) will be gated out and only caught later, which is an accepted false-negative cost to keep precision high; and w_recency/tau are set by the staleness argument, not estimated from the data, so the exact down-weighting is a judgment parameter. The rule is a triage heuristic, not a guarantee: it ranks and budgets, it does not confirm.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4: Address how the model could be updated given additional new reports over time, and how often the updates should occur.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) New reports arrive continuously (the event-driven process of Subproblem 1) but only the processed subset (Positive/Negative ID) adds confirmed labels usable to refit. (b) The model's parameters (logistic coefficients, the 30 km gate, the threshold, the seasonal weights) are fixed structural choices; what is updated is the trained weight vector and the running statistics. (c) Updates should be frequent enough that the prioritization reflects the current spatial footprint and base rate, but not so frequent that the model is refit on negligible new evidence. Method: a two-part update policy. (1) Parameter update: refit the logistic model whenever the number of newly processed reports since the last fit exceeds a fraction of the current processed set (a relative-increment rule) OR on a fixed weekly cadence, whichever comes first. (2) State update: the set of confirmed positives (hence the proximity gate centers and the 30 km radii) is updated immediately as each positive is confirmed, because a new positive changes which reports are 'near a known detection' and therefore which are actionable. The base rate and its interval are recomputed at each fit.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let P_t be the number of processed reports available at time t and let p_t = (positives among processed)/(total processed). Refit trigger: fit a new model at time t when (processed_t - processed_{lastfit}) > 0.10 * processed_{lastfit} OR (t - t_{lastfit}) >= 1 week. On refit, recompute the standardized coefficients beta, the threshold, and the Wilson 95% CI for p_t: [ beta.ppf(0.025; k, n-k+1), beta.ppf(0.975; k+1, n-k) ] where k = positives, n = processed. The proximity gate is updated non-parametrically: upon each new confirmed positive, add its location as a new 30 km gate center. The seasonal weights and the recency half-scale tau are held fixed unless a full seasonal cycle shows systematic miscalibration. Rationale for frequency: the 10% relative-increment bound means the model is not refit on noise (a handful of new reports) but is refit as the confirmed footprint grows, while the weekly floor ensures the model does not go stale during a quiet period. During an active burst, the weekly floor and the immediate positive-gate update together keep the triage current week by week.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: This is an incremental, label-driven update scheme: the expensive refit is gated on meaningful new labels, while the cheap but decision-critical spatial state (the gate centers) updates in real time. At the current data scale (2,069 processed, 14 positives) the 10% rule would trigger a refit after ~207 newly processed reports, which during the 2020 burst is reached within days, so effectively the model tracks the burst weekly. Limitations: with so few positives, each new positive substantially shifts the base rate and the gate, so the model is sensitive to small label additions and the intervals are wide early on; the 10% and weekly constants are policy choices, not estimates, and should be tuned to the agency's actual processing throughput; and retrospective backfilled reports (old detections reported late) can mis-date the label arrival, so the 'time' axis of the update is submission/processing time, not detection time.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 5: Using the model, define what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) Eradication is the absence of surviving, reproducing colonies, so the observable signature is the absence of confirmed positives over a period long enough that a still-present pest would almost certainly have produced at least one detection. (b) Detection is imperfect: in any given season there is a probability D of detecting a present pest in the endemic zone, and a probability 1-D of missing it. (c) The detection process is seasonal, because the pest is active and findable mainly in the spring-summer foraging season (fertilized queens emerge in spring; new queens disperse in fall). Method: a sequential absence-of-events argument. Model the number of confirmed positives observed in a season, given the pest is present, as a Bernoulli detection with success probability D (at least one detection). Over K consecutive seasons with zero confirmed positives, the probability of having missed the pest every season (a false all-clear) is (1-D)^K. Eradication is declared when this false-all-clear probability falls below a chosen significance alpha (0.05). D is calibrated to the endemic-zone detection efficacy observed in the data (the Blaine cluster produced multiple confirmations within a single season once searching was targeted, supporting D in the 0.5-0.7 range; a conservative D=0.3 is also reported). The criterion is combined with negative active surveillance, not passive reports alone, because passive reporting is alarm-driven and unreliable as a negative test.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let D = P(at least one confirmed detection in a season | pest present in the zone), K = number of consecutive full seasonal cycles (spring-through-fall) with zero confirmed positives in the endemic zone plus targeted negative surveillance. False-all-clear probability = (1-D)^K. Declare eradication when (1-D)^K <= alpha = 0.05, i.e. K >= ceil( log(0.05) / log(1-D) ). Calibrated values: D=0.3 -> K=9 seasons (P miss = 0.040); D=0.5 -> K=5 seasons (P miss = 0.031); D=0.7 -> K=3 seasons (P miss = 0.027). A defensible primary criterion is therefore: zero confirmed positives for 5 consecutive full seasons (under a moderate D=0.5, giving a 3.1% chance of a false all-clear) in the endemic zone, supported by negative active surveillance (trapping/inspections with no recovery) and no new positive gate centers. The base positive rate and its 95% CI [0.0037, 0.0113] bracket the detection sensitivity used to choose D.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The eradication claim is a statement about a lower bound on the probability of undetected persistence, made explicit rather than assumed: after 5 silent seasons the chance the pest is still present but undetected is ~3%, and after 9 silent seasons it is ~4% even under a pessimistic D=0.3 (the K grows because 1-D is larger, offset by more seasons; the bound is tightest at moderate D). Limitations and biases: (a) D is not directly measurable from the data (there is no known-present ground truth to calibrate against), so it is a sensitivity parameter and the answer is given as a range over D rather than a single number; (b) passive public reports alone are an inadequate negative test because they are alarm-driven and sparse, so the criterion explicitly requires active surveillance; (c) a re-introduction from outside (e.g. from British Columbia, where the Nanaimo colony existed) is not ruled out by historical silence, so the criterion applies to the current endemic zone and should be re-armed if a new positive gate center appears; (d) the seasonal-cycle definition (spring-fall) means a 'season' is roughly 12 months, so 5 seasons is a ~5-year horizon, which is long but appropriate for a pest whose colonies are hard to find when absent.
